newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr climb pauses as heights dizzy.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr climb pauses as heights dizzy.

text.p: The Australian dollar took a breather at 80 cents Tuesday as its recent sprint up to three month highs left some feeling dizzy.
Dealers said the currency had run into profit-taking atop the 80 level and would-be buyers were discouraged by talk of a big options-related sell order from an Asian bank at US$0.8020.
There was also a feeling the dollar had pulled too far ahead of fundamentals, particularly commodity prices which were yet to show the strength bulls were counting on.
Nevertheless, Japanese and U.S. enthusiasm for the high yielder seemed unabated leading most to expect further gains.

By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar was resting at US$0.7998/03 from an early US$0.7986/91 and US$0.8002/07 late here Monday. That was off from Monday's US$0.8021 peak, but still far above last Tuesday's US$0.7913/18 finish.

Support was pencilled in at US$0.7980 and US$0.7950 where a former downtrend line provided a solid chart base. Resistance was to be found at US$0.8020 but the technically more meaningful level was US$0.8050, that being a 5-1/2 year peak from May.
It had a see saw session on the crosses as early talk of buying for a dual currency samurai issue lifted the dollar on the yen, only for it to be restrained by Japanese rate jitters.

The latter followed a stunningly strong 13.6 percent rise in July Japanese private machinery orders. That suggested capital investment was running strongly and reminded the market that Japanese rates could not stay at record low levels for ever.

Government officials played down the figures, however, and analysts remained confident that no tightening would come until the new year. That helped the local dollar hold steady at 87.32/42 yen from 87.30/40 late Monday. In trade weighted terms it eased to 58.7 from 58.8.
Strong domestic economic data also provided support by making a rate cut here look a little less likely.
Housing finance commitments jumped 16 percent in July, dwarfing forecasts of a 4.7 percent gain and more than making up for falls in May and June.
Analysts said the data were not quite as strong as they seemed since much of the gain was due to a 25 percent jump in refinancing, which accounted for a quarter of all commitments.

However, commitments for the purchase of existing dwellings rose a healthy 15 percent suggesting the outbreak of competitive reductions in commercial bank mortgage rates seen in July had at least injected some life into the long dormant housing market.
And mortgage rates had been cut further since then following the RBA's reduction in official rates on July 31, raising the prospect of another upbeat month in August.

"If there continue to be suggestions of a strong and immediate rise in the housing sector, as opposed to a gentle upturn, the RBA will be reluctant to ease again," said Grant Bailey, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
But the jump in commitments alone would not stay the RBA's hand given its emphasis on reducing unemployment, analysts said.
That made Thursday's jobs data for August a more important release as far as monetary policy was concerned.

The risk of a weak employment outcome would make the market cautious of chasing the local dollar higher, especially as some analysts were nudging down their forecasts after the surprise fall seen in August ANZ job advertisement figures on Monday.
However, analysts thought it unlikely the data would be so dire as to justify another cut before key inflation and wages were out in late October, leaving the dollar wellplaced for now.

"The A$ outlook remains flat to bullish -- there appear to be few reasons why it should weaken," said Citibank's Bailey. "A test of the six year high above US$0.8050 looks assured in the near term." -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
